title: Technical deep dive: Observability & OpenTelemetry token-level metrics
summary: Redwood SE team walked Atlas Media through OpenTelemetry integration for token-level metrics and tracing. Discussed tradeoffs for token-level spans vs aggregated metrics, sample OTLP configuration, cardinality controls, KV cache and batching metrics, overhead estimates, and on-prem/VPC considerations. Agreed next steps: share integration guide, run a 1-week pilot with token sampling enabled, and schedule follow-up benchmark run with Atlas's dev environment.
topics: VPC/on-prem OTLP endpoints and firewall considerations

Atlas to provision OTLP endpoint or agree on Redwood-hosted OTLP proxy for pilot
Marco to run 3 synthetic runs and share latency/cost delta (with token metrics on/off)
Schedule follow-up in 2 weeks to review pilot results

transcript:
[00:00:00] Sarah (Redwood AE): hey everyone thanks for jumping on we, um, wanted to run through the observability deep dive for token-level metrics and OpenTe--- OpenTelemetry integration. quick intro - marco is our SE on inference perf, aisha on product.
[00:00:25] Priya (Atlas): hi thanks, Priya here. we've got Ethan and Lily and Tom as well. main goal is to understand overheads and how we can debug latency spikes down to tokens if needed.
[00:00:45] Marco (Redwood SE): cool, i'll start with high-level. two approaches we recommend: aggregated metrics (per-request and per-token counters emitted at batch end) vs trace-heavy approach (span per token). there's tradeoffs: span-per-token gives best trace-level visibility but explosion in cardinality and exporter load.
[00:01:10] Ethan (Atlas): when you say explosion how big are we talking? we expect 1k rps during peak, average 60 tokens per request.
[00:01:27] Marco (SE): so naive span-per-token is 60k spans per second — pretty expensive. that's why we often do sampling or we emit token-level metrics like tokens_generated_total, tokens_tokenized_total, kv_cache_hits_total and a token_latency histogram aggregated by request_id. that gives you p50/p95 token latency without a span for every token.
[00:01:55] Lily (Sec): and what about PII? token-level payloads could leak sensitive data in traces.
[00:02:08] Aisha (Product): yes good point— we mask token text by default; redwood only emits counts and latency numbers. we never emit raw tokens in telemetry unless explicitly enabled for debugging with strict access.
[00:02:30] Tom (SRE): how's this look over a VPC/private setup? we have strict egress rules.
[00:02:40] Sarah (AE): we support two patterns: send OTLP to your in-VPC collector (preferred), or use a Redwood-hosted proxy with TLS and mTLS. For on-prem, we can run a lightweight OTLP proxy in your DMZ. we'll share sample configs.
[00:03:05] Marco: quick slide — metric names we recommend: redwood_inference_requests_total, redwood_tokens_generated_total, redwood_kv_cache_hits_total, redwood_kv_cache_misses_total, redwood_batch_size_histogram, redwood_inference_latency_seconds (summary/pcts), redwood_token_latency_seconds_bucket (if you need token histograms). we also attach resource attributes: deployment, model_name, model_variant, quantization, gpu_type, customer_id. be mindful of high-cardinality attributes like request_id — keep those in traces not metrics.
[00:03:45] Priya: can you show an example OTLP yaml?
[00:03:50] Marco: yeah i'll paste a sample after — but key bits: use OTLP/gRPC export with tls certs, set a resource detector for k8s/pod, and use a batcher with a 200ms max delay for metrics. for traces, lower batch delay increases latency to destination but improves timeliness. also use aggregation boundaries to reduce cardinality.
[00:04:20] [00:04:20] Sarah: (interrupt) quick note on sampling: we suggest dynamic sampling at the edge — e.g., 1% full token-span sampling plus 100% event-level traces (request start/end) for all requests. that gives you ability to drill into sampled traces.
[00:04:40] Ethan: what's the CPU overhead on the inference node for token-level metrics?
[00:04:47] Marco: with our runtime, emitting aggregated counters and a per-request token histogram is lightweight — typically <3% CPU overhead and ~2-4% latency increase at p95 for small models. full span-per-token approach can be 20-30% CPU and network cost. numbers depend on batch sizes and quantization.
[00:05:12] Priya: can you talk about kv cache metrics? we need to know when cache is cold.
[00:05:18] Aisha: we emit kv_cache_hits_total and kv_cache_misses_total with labels for model and customer. a useful derived metric is kv_cache_hit_rate = hits / (hits + misses). also emit kv_cache_latency_seconds_histogram for cache lookup times. when cache miss spikes, you'll often see increased token latency and downstream higher GPU utilization.
[00:05:45] Tom: we already have Prometheus and Grafana in-house — can we scrape the metrics directly?
[00:05:52] Marco: yes, our recommendation: run an OTEL Collector in your VPC, export OTLP->Prometheus. Alternatively Redwood can send metrics to your Prometheus remote_write endpoint. For VPC/on-prem it's usually: 1) collector in-cluster; 2) configure redwood to push OTLP to that collector over mTLS.
[00:06:20] [00:06:20] Priya: any guidance on dashboards/alerts? what should we set p95 thresholds on?
[00:06:28] Sarah: baseline: p50 token latency is useful for user perceived snappiness; p95/p99 token latency exposed per-model and per-route. also set alerts on kv_cache_hit_rate drops, batch_size deviations (sudden drop can indicate routing change), and inference error_rate. for cost control, token generation rate per minute is helpful.
[00:06:55] Lily (Sec): audit logs — do traces include user identifiable info or API keys?
[00:07:02] Marco: all telemetry we emit is metadata-only by default: no API keys or raw prompt text. For audit logs we can emit request IDs and action markers but we recommend shipping full logs to your secure SIEM rather than Redwood.
[00:07:20] Ethan: quantization — does int8 or 4-bit quantization change telemetry behavior? any gotchas?
[00:07:28] Marco: quantization mostly affects kernel runtimes and latency distributions; metrics names have a quantization label so you can compare. one gotcha: quantized paths can show different token latency variance, so your token latency histogram buckets may need tuning. also some internal batching heuristics change, impacting batch size histograms.
[00:07:58] Sarah: demo time — Marco, can you show the sample Grafana dashboard we shipped in the deck?
[00:08:03] Marco: sure sharing screen now (note: transcript may not capture slides).
[00:08:15] [00:08:15] Marco: here's the dashboard — top row: request rate, tokens per second, error rate. middle: latency panels (inference p50/p95/p99) broken down by model and quantization. bottom row: kv cache hit rate and batch size heatmap.
[00:08:45] Priya: how are you computing token-level p95? is it aggregated in the collector or by Redwood?
[00:08:52] Marco: we emit token latency histograms from the runtime (bucketed) and the collector aggregates them. we also ship pre-aggregated p50/p95 metrics if you want less cardinality.
[00:09:10] Ethan: sample queries to correlate traces with metrics? like find requests with high p95 and then jump to trace.
[00:09:18] Marco: best practice: each request has a request_id that you include as a trace_id attribute. In Grafana you can add a link to the trace explorer with ?trace_id=${request_id}. we provide a small panel that surfaces top request_ids by token p95.
[00:09:35] Tom: ok but how do we keep cardinality low if we attach user id and route in metrics?
[00:09:43] Marco: use route/model labels — route is coarse (api.chat, api.embed). avoid per-user labels on metrics. For traces, you can attach user id as an attribute if you have RBAC and limited retention.
[00:09:58] [00:09:58] Priya: maybe show synthetics — what's the benchmark delta when token-mode is on.
[00:10:05] Marco: last internal test: turning on full token histograms increased network egress ~15% and CPU ~6% for our default load. p95 latency increased by ~8ms on a 100ms baseline. with sampling (1% spans + aggregated metrics) overhead <2%.
[00:10:30] Lily: how long do you retain telemetry by default?
[00:10:35] Aisha: Redwood stores aggregated metrics for 90 days by default for hosted customers; traces are sampled and stored for 30 days unless you request longer. For Private deployments, retention is controlled by the customer collector/back-end.
[00:10:52] Priya: on the collector config, any recommended processor chain?
[00:10:56] Marco: yes: resource detector -> attributes processor (add model labels) -> batch processor (metrics) -> memory_limiter -> exporter. For traces, add a tail-sampling extension if you want to sample based on downstream errors or latency.
[00:11:20] [00:11:20] Sarah: let's talk firewall/egress: Tom — can you confirm whether you can open outbound to a Redwood proxy or you prefer in-VPC collector?
[00:11:28] Tom: we prefer in-VPC; we'd rather not open general outbound.
[00:11:33] Sarah: great; we'll provide the OTLP endpoint and a sample helm chart for the collector.
[00:11:40] Marco: follow-up on dashboards: suggest panels for token_latency_seconds p50/p95, bucketed histogram heatmap, kv_cache_hit_rate, batch_size_percentile, tokens_generated_per_minute, and GPU_utilization.
[00:11:58] Priya: any tips for alert thresholds? p95 > 2x baseline?
[00:12:02] Marco: yes — use baseline behavior: set alert if p95 > 1.5x baseline sustained for 3 minutes. another useful alert: sudden drop in batch size by >30% which often indicates routing misconfig or throttling.
[00:12:20] Ethan: one operational question: can we correlate model rollouts with telemetry? we do canaries.
[00:12:27] Aisha: we tag metrics with model_version and rollout_id so canary vs stable are visible. we also have automated SLO checks that can trigger rollbacks if quality metrics degrade.
[00:12:40] [00:12:40] Tom: sample log linkage — how to find full request payload?
[00:12:45] Marco: request_id is in metrics and traces; logs with that request_id in your logging system will tie them. Redwood can emit the request_id in the response header if you want.
[00:12:58] Priya: do you provide example Grafana dashboards or do we need to build from scratch?
[00:13:03] Sarah: we provide starter dashboards and panels in JSON; we'll share the repo link in the follow-up.
[00:13:12] [00:13:12] Ethan: security: mTLS — do you support client cert rotation?
[00:13:17] Marco: yes, certificate rotation via ACME or your internal CA — we have docs for cert lifecycle and a sample automation script.
[00:13:30] Lily: retention and data residency again — for Private deployments we want everything to never leave our VPC; can Redwood still give aggregated dashboards?
[00:13:40] Sarah: for Private, you run the collector and metrics store in your environment; Redwood's console can optionally display metrics via a read-only dashboard pulled over a secure connection if you opt in, otherwise you keep data on-prem.
[00:13:58] Priya: question about tokenization differences across models — does metrics unify token counts across GPT-style vs others?
[00:14:04] Marco: we standardize on token metrics at the runtime layer and include tokenizer_name label. when comparing models, normalize by tokens per second and token latency.
[00:14:20] [00:14:20] Sarah: demo over, let's do Q&A.
[00:14:24] Priya: ok we have an integration question — our org requires low-cardinality metrics. can you provide pre-aggregated metrics only and skip histograms?
[00:14:32] Marco: yes, you can configure runtime flags to only emit counters and pre-computed p50/p95. that reduces cardinality and exporter load.
[00:14:46] Ethan: do you support prometheus remote_write for long term storage?
[00:14:50] Marco: yes. Redwood can export to your remote_write endpoint or you can collect OTLP in your collector and forward to remote_write.
[00:15:05] Lily: any integration with OpenSearch/Elastic for traces?
[00:15:09] Marco: OTLP collector supports exporters to Elastic APM/Opensearch as well; we'll add sample config.
[00:15:22] Priya: can we get more detail on the token_latency_seconds buckets? recommended boundaries?
[00:15:27] Marco: a good start: [0.0001, 0.001, 0.005, 0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2] seconds — adjust based on model.
[00:15:48] [00:15:48] Tom: there's a comment in our ticket about tail latencies — how to debug 99.9th percentile spikes that happen rarely?
[00:15:55] Marco: tail sampling helps — capture full token spans for requests that exceed a latency threshold, e.g., trace if request latency > 2s. that, combined with kv_cache and GPU metrics, usually reveals root cause. we also recommend capturing system metrics (cpu, mem, disk IO) at 1s granularity during experiments.
[00:16:20] Priya: how do you correlate GPU kernel stalls with token latency?
[00:16:25] Marco: we emit gpu_utilization and kernel_queue_depth metrics and associate them with model_name and request_id; a sudden rise in kernel_queue_depth with stable request rate is an indicator of backpressure.
[00:16:38] [00:16:38] Sarah: ok time check — we've got about 40 minutes left. anything else from Atlas?
[00:16:45] Priya: timeline — we want to pilot next week in dev and then decide for prod in 3 weeks.
[00:16:50] Sarah: sounds good. immediate deliverables we'll send: integration guide, helm chart, starter Grafana dash, and benchmark script.
[00:17:06] Ethan: will you include examples for prom remote_write and OTLP collector in the repo?
[00:17:10] Marco: yes.
[00:17:18] Tom: about cost — if we enable token-level telemetry full time will that increase billing from Redwood?
[00:17:25] Sarah: for hosted customers additional telemetry can slightly increase metering; for Dedicated/Private it's typically the customer's infra cost. we'll put estimates in the follow-up.
[00:17:40] [00:17:40] Priya: any gotchas for autoscaling? metrics delay can hide quick spikes.
[00:17:46] Marco: use shorter scrape intervals for metrics tied to autoscaling, and instrument fallback policies in Redwood so we have quick signals when autoscaler kicks in.
[00:18:00] Lily: legal — if we need to export telemetry to a partner, how do we get consent?
[00:18:05] Sarah: we'd treat that as a data processing arrangement; we can restrict telemetry fields and provide an export policy. we'll coordinate with your legal.
[00:18:20] [00:18:20] Marco: ok i'm going to paste a short sample OTEL collector config in the chat (transcript paraphrases):
[00:18:30] Marco: ---
receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      grpc: {}
processors:
  batch:
exporters:
  prometheusremotewrite:
    endpoint: 'https://prom-remote.write.example'
  otlp/secure:
    endpoint: '${OTLP_ENDPOINT}'
    tls:
      ca_file: /etc/otel/ca.pem
service:
  pipelines:
    metrics:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [batch]
      exporters: [prometheusremotewrite, otlp/secure]
---
[00:19:10] Priya: thanks — that helps.
[00:19:15] Marco: also, use a memory_limiter to avoid collector OOMs if you enable full token spans.
[00:19:25] [00:19:25] Priya: are there examples of Grafana alerts for batch-size anomalies?
[00:19:31] Sarah: yes we'll include a sample alert rule: when avg(batch_size) over 5m drops by >30% relative to 30m baseline.
[00:19:45] Ethan: ok let's talk pilot acceptance criteria — what do we need to validate?
[00:19:51] Marco: acceptance: 1) token-level metrics visible in Atlas Grafana, 2) KV cache hit rate metric present and instrumented, 3) observed overhead <5% CPU and <10% network egress increase for aggregated metrics, 4) ability to link traces to logs via request_id.
[00:20:15] Lily: we'll need an internal security review for the sample configs.
[00:20:19] Sarah: understoood — we'll send docs for the security review.
[00:20:28] [00:20:28] Priya: a quick question on instrumentation for dedicated infer nodes — are metrics emitted per process or per container?
[00:20:35] Marco: per process, but we surface container and pod labels via resource detectors so you can aggregate per node.
[00:20:50] Ethan: what about batching — does the runtime expose batch composition metrics?
[00:20:56] Marco: yes: redwood_batch_size_histogram, batch_compose_time_seconds, and batch_wait_time_seconds. these help you understand queueing and tail behavior.
[00:21:15] Priya: if during pilot we see increased tail latency, who do we call?
[00:21:19] Sarah: AE and SE on-call for pilot. we'll provide a slack channel and a runbook for triage.
[00:21:30] [00:21:30] Tom: one last nit — is there a way to instrument token compression metrics when using caching and re-use?
[00:21:36] Marco: yes we emit tokens_reused_total and tokens_from_cache_total; combined with token_latency you can tell the benefit of caching.
[00:21:50] Priya: ok let's recap next steps.
[00:21:54] Sarah: recap: Sarah share integration guide, helm chart, starter dashboards and alert rules by 2026-07-20. Marco run synthetic benchmarks and share numbers by 2026-07-22. Atlas to stand up collector or provide endpoint by 2026-07-19. follow up call in 2 weeks.
[00:22:20] [00:22:20] Ethan: thanks all. small side noise — sorry if i mis-said some acronyms earlier.
[00:22:28] Sarah: no worries. we'll add the deck and repo link to the follow-up email.
[00:22:35] Priya: thanks everyone.
